body:
Economic life under the Mughals

The Mughal Empire was one of the major political and economic powers of Asia during the 16th and 17th centuries. Its economy depended primarily on agriculture, but it also supported extensive craft production, flourishing towns, inland markets and international trade.

Most people lived in villages. Cultivators produced food grains and commercial crops, artisans manufactured goods, merchants transported and sold these products, and the state collected a substantial share of agricultural production as revenue.

In the 16th and 17th centuries, approximately 85% of India's population lived in villages. This figure illustrates the importance of the countryside, but it does not mean that the economy was isolated from towns or markets. Villages supplied agricultural produce, raw materials and labour to the wider economy.

How agriculture supported the empire

Land revenue was the principal financial foundation of the Mughal state. The revenue collected from cultivation supported the imperial household, administration, military establishments and the officials who served the emperor.

Revenue and markets connected different groups. A cultivator might grow wheat for household consumption and cotton for sale. A merchant could purchase the cotton, a weaver could turn it into cloth, and another merchant could sell that cloth in an Indian town or overseas. Money earned from such transactions circulated through rural and urban markets.

Principal economic and social groups

  • Peasants or raiyats: People who cultivated agricultural land, either as resident cultivators or as cultivators working elsewhere.
  • Zamindars: Local landed elites who possessed property and often exercised rights connected with revenue collection.
  • Artisans: Skilled producers such as weavers, potters, carpenters, metalworkers and stone carvers.
  • Merchants and bankers: People who organised trade, credit, money exchange and the movement of goods.
  • Mansabdars and jagirdars: Imperial officials who received salaries or assignments of revenue in return for service.

These groups did not form separate, self-contained economies. Their activities overlapped. Peasant households sometimes manufactured goods, zamindars established markets, merchants financed production, and imperial demand encouraged specialised crafts.

Two important characteristics

First, Mughal agriculture combined subsistence production, which provided food for daily needs, with commercial production, which supplied markets and generated income.

Second, both payment in kind and monetary transactions existed. The presence of harvest-sharing arrangements does not mean that the Mughal economy operated entirely through barter. Cash revenue, wages, credit and silver currency were important, particularly in commercially connected regions.

Prelims focus

  • Approximately 85% of the population lived in villages during the 16th and 17th centuries.
  • Land revenue was the principal source of income for the Mughal state.
  • Agriculture supplied both food crops and raw materials for crafts and trade.
  • Commercial agriculture, cash transactions and overseas trade existed alongside village production.
  • Trap: A predominantly agricultural economy was not necessarily an economy without trade or money.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, printed pp. 196–198, 205–206 and 213–216; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, printed pp. 52–56.]

title: The Mughal Economy: Agriculture, Revenue and Trade

body:
The peasant as the principal producer

The village was the basic unit of agricultural production. Peasants tilled fields, sowed seeds, removed weeds, harvested crops and performed the other seasonal tasks required for cultivation. Their households also contributed labour to activities such as oil pressing, sugar production and textile preparation.

Persian administrative sources commonly used the term raiyat for a peasant. Other terms included muzarian, kisan and asami.

Resident and non-resident cultivators

  • Khud-kashta: Peasants who resided in the village where they held and cultivated their land.
  • Pahi-kashta: Peasants who belonged to another village but cultivated land elsewhere, often under a contractual arrangement.

A person might become a pahi-kashta cultivator to obtain more favourable terms of cultivation. Migration could also result from distress, including famine. Thus, Mughal rural society included both settled cultivators and people who moved in search of livelihood.

Agricultural seasons and crops

Farming was organised around 2 principal seasonal cycles: kharif and rabi. Kharif crops depended chiefly on the monsoon and were generally harvested in autumn. Rabi crops were normally sown after the monsoon and harvested in spring.

Rice, wheat and millets were major food crops. Rice was especially associated with areas receiving abundant rainfall, while wheat and millets were important in other climatic conditions. The exact combination of crops depended on rainfall, soil, irrigation and local agricultural practices.

Commercial crops

Food production was not the only purpose of cultivation. Peasants also grew crops for sale. Mughal sources used the expression jins-i kamil, literally meaning excellent or perfect crops, for valuable crops that could generate higher revenue.

Cotton and sugarcane were important examples. Cotton supplied the textile industry, while sugarcane supported sugar production. Oilseeds, indigo and other crops also entered commercial exchange. A household could therefore grow food grains and marketable crops on the same holding.

Irrigation and agricultural technology

Monsoon rainfall remained essential to agriculture, but irrigation supported cultivation where rainfall was insufficient or irregular. Wells, tanks and canals supplied additional water. In parts of northern India, cultivators used the Persian wheel, a device in which an animal-powered mechanism raised water from a well using a continuous chain of containers.

The state sometimes supported irrigation works. During Shah Jahan's reign, older canals were repaired and new works undertaken, including improvements associated with the shahnahr in Punjab.

Common agricultural implements included a wooden plough, often fitted with an iron tip, and tools for weeding. Agriculture was labour-intensive, but cultivators used available technology and animal power rather than relying exclusively on manual digging.

New crops and changing consumption

Commercial contacts introduced additional crops into India. Maize was cultivated in parts of western India by the 17th century. Tobacco spread during the early 17th century, while crops of American origin such as potatoes, tomatoes and chillies also entered the subcontinent.

The Ain-i Akbari does not list tobacco among the northern Indian crops recorded during Akbar's reign. This is useful evidence for distinguishing established crops from those that became more widespread during the 17th century.

Prelims focus

  • Raiyat was a common term for a peasant.
  • Khud-kashta referred to resident cultivators; pahi-kashta referred to cultivators working away from their home villages.
  • Kharif was associated with monsoon cultivation; rabi crops were generally harvested in spring.
  • Cotton and sugarcane were important examples of jins-i kamil.
  • The Persian wheel helped lift irrigation water from wells.
  • Trap: Mughal agriculture included commercial crops; it was not exclusively subsistence farming.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, printed pp. 196–201, sections 1.2–1.4, including the accounts of irrigation and crop cultivation.]

title: Mughal Agriculture: Peasants, Crops and Irrigation

body:
The village as a community

A Mughal village was more than a collection of agricultural fields. Its residents participated in cultivation, craft production, exchange, social regulation and the management of shared resources.

Three important components of the village community were the cultivators, the village panchayat and the village headman.

Village panchayat and headman

The village panchayat was an assembly of elders, usually drawn from influential village families. It settled disputes, regulated social conduct and sometimes supervised the use of common funds for community needs, such as repairs or protection against natural calamities.

The headman was known as the muqaddam or mandal. In some areas, village elders selected the headman and a zamindar confirmed the choice. The headman helped supervise village affairs and accounts.

The patwari maintained village accounts and land-related records. His work assisted the assessment and collection of revenue.

Artisans and service relationships

Many villages contained specialised artisans, including potters, blacksmiths, carpenters, barbers and weavers. A blacksmith repaired agricultural tools; a carpenter made implements and wooden structures; a potter supplied household vessels.

Artisans could receive grain, a share of the harvest, land or money in return for their services. Some agreements operated between individual households and artisans; others involved the village community.

Such hereditary or customary service relationships later came to be described as the jajmani system. However, the term jajmani should not be treated as the universal contemporary name for these arrangements during the 16th and 17th centuries.

Caste, occupation and inequality

Rural society was divided by differences of caste, occupation, wealth and access to land. Some families possessed substantial holdings, while others worked as agricultural labourers or performed services that received low social status.

Although panchayats could represent more than one caste or community, they were not modern democratic institutions based on equal adult participation. Influential households often dominated decisions, and poorer workers might have little representation.

Women's contribution to production

Women played a major role in agriculture and crafts. Their work included sowing, weeding, threshing, winnowing, spinning, embroidery and preparing materials for artisanal production.

Customs concerning marriage, property and employment varied among social groups. Some women from landed families inherited property, and women could hold or manage zamindari interests. These examples do not mean that women generally enjoyed the same rights and authority as men.

Forest dwellers, pastoralists and mobile communities

Mughal society also included people who lived outside settled agricultural villages. Forest communities depended on combinations of hunting, gathering, fishing, shifting cultivation and trade in forest products.

The Bhils, for example, practised different livelihood activities according to the season. Forest products such as honey, wax and lac entered wider trading networks. Some tribal chiefs acquired zamindari rights or developed political authority over larger territories.

Pastoral communities supplied animals and animal products. Mobile traders transported goods between villages, towns and distant markets. These groups formed part of the economy even when they were not permanent residents of cultivated villages.

The description of a village as a self-sufficient or equal community is misleading. Mughal villages had inequalities of wealth and status, and they maintained economic connections with towns and markets.

Prelims focus

  • Muqaddam or mandal: village headman.
  • Patwari: village accountant and record keeper.
  • Village panchayats were assemblies of elders, not modern elected local governments.
  • Artisans could be paid in grain, land or cash.
  • Women participated in both agricultural and craft production.
  • Forest products and pastoral activities were part of the wider Mughal economy.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, printed pp. 201–211, sections 2–4; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 7, Tribes, Nomads and Settled Communities.]

pictures.alt: Cultivators produce crops, artisans supply goods and services, panchayat elders handle village affairs, the headman leads, and the patwari keeps accounts.
pictures.caption: Village institutions and occupational groups.

title: Village Communities and the Social Structure of Mughal India

body:
Who were the zamindars?

In Mughal India, zamindars were influential rural proprietors who held land and enjoyed social, economic and sometimes military privileges. Many also possessed customary rights connected with collecting revenue on behalf of the state.

Zamindars were not necessarily the people who personally cultivated all the land under their influence. Cultivation was usually performed by peasants and labourers, while zamindars exercised rights over property, revenue and local authority.

Milkiyat: privately held property

The personal lands of zamindars were called milkiyat. These lands could be cultivated using hired or dependent labour. Zamindars could sell, mortgage or bequeath their milkiyat property.

Some zamindars maintained fortified residences and armed followers. Their military resources strengthened their position in dealings with neighbouring chiefs and imperial officials.

How zamindars obtained income and influence

Zamindars could derive income from cultivation on their own lands, from recognised revenue rights and from other local economic activities. Some assisted agricultural expansion by settling cultivators, providing loans or supporting the development of new lands.

They also established or encouraged markets known as haats, where peasants and merchants could exchange produce.

Zamindar, jagirdar and peasant: different positions

GroupMain economic positionEssential distinction
PeasantCultivated land and produced crops.Direct agricultural producer.
ZamindarHeld local property and often revenue-collection rights.Had established interests in a locality.
JagirdarReceived an imperial assignment of revenue as remuneration for service.A jagir was a revenue assignment, not automatic private ownership of all land in the assigned area.

A mansabdar was an imperial officer whose rank helped determine status, pay and military obligations. A mansabdar might receive payment in cash or through a jagir. A jagirdar could therefore collect revenue from an assigned territory without owning every cultivator's field or possessing the hereditary local rights of its zamindars.

Cooperation and conflict

The relationship between zamindars, peasants and the state was not always peaceful. Revenue demands could create disputes among cultivators, local elites and imperial collectors.

Yet zamindars and peasants were not always opponents. When state demands threatened their shared local interests, they sometimes acted together against imperial officials. In other circumstances, a zamindar's own demands might become a source of pressure on cultivators.

Prelims focus

  • Milkiyat referred to the personal property lands of zamindars.
  • Zamindars often exercised local revenue rights and possessed social influence.
  • A jagir was an assignment of revenue connected with imperial service.
  • Peasants were the direct cultivators of agricultural land.
  • Zamindars sometimes helped settle cultivators and establish markets.
  • Trap: Zamindar and jagirdar were not interchangeable terms.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, printed pp. 211–214, sections 5–6; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, section Mansabdars and Jagirdars.]

pictures.alt: Zamindars may help collect revenue and settle peasants, but excessive demands can cause disputes and joint resistance to imperial officials.
pictures.caption: Rural relations combined cooperation and conflict.
